summary: NVIDIA Research's HORIZON: a user-written Markdown harness (objective, domain knowledge, evaluator, acceptance predicate) is compiled by a bootstrap agent into a 'project pack'. A hands-free GPT-5.3 loop then edits an isolated git worktree, runs the evaluator, and commits or logs each attempt, with git history serving as the trace. A single run reaches 100% on ChipBench, RTLLM-2.0, Verilog-Eval v2 and nine CVDP categories. The acceptance gate is each benchmark's own scoring harness, whose failure logs the agent can read, so the 100% means the agent converged on the visible grader.

claims.claim: HORIZON achieves 100% benchmark completion across all suites
claims.evidence: Table 1, single run. The acceptance predicate is the benchmark's pass condition, and the agent sees the harness's simulator messages and failure traces (§4, §5). No hidden or held-out tests exist, which the authors call an 'over-solving or reward-hacking failure mode'. ChipBench shows 100.0 with footnote (a): one task still fails, and 'counting it as resolved yields 100%'.

claims.claim: First agentic system to complete all evaluated RTL suites end-to-end without human intervention
claims.evidence: No baseline is run. The prior agentic RTL systems listed in §2 (AutoChip, VerilogCoder, MAGE, ACE-RTL) are not evaluated under the same unlimited-iteration, grader-visible protocol. Iteration-0 numbers are explicitly not Pass@1.

claims.claim: Token cost is concentrated in a few hard CVDP categories, and about 91% of tokens are cached input
claims.evidence: Table 2: 209.9M tokens in total, CID 002 alone 56.0M, the three legacy suites 6.0M. Single run; no dollar cost.

claims.claim: Generated testbench stimulus is substantive: coverage rises from 86.5% to 97.9% on CID 012
claims.evidence: Table 3 and Fig. 4 cover two categories; for CID 014, coverage is averaged over the 60 parsed logs only.

patterns.note: Domain knowledge (invariants, tool conventions, failure modes) is written in the Markdown harness and compiled into 'domain skills'. There is no ablation without the domain knowledge.

An evaluator-gated commit/reject loop. Because the gate is the benchmark grader, the paper cannot separate genuine repair from fitting to the grader. No comparison is made with a single attempt under the same budget.
Each task runs in an isolated git worktree. All reported results are single-agent; no parallel agents are evaluated.
Git commits and notes store evaluator verdicts as a replayable trace. Not evaluated.
The authors themselves argue RTL benchmarks need hidden randomized tests or formal checks separated from repair-time feedback (§5).

methodology.sample: ChipBench, RTLLM-2.0, Verilog-Eval v2, CVDP CID 002-016 (nine categories); per-suite task counts are not tabulated
methodology.contamination_controls: None. Final scoring uses the same harness the agent repaired against

standards.artifacts: None released; the only link is the public SWE-bench experiments repo

biases.detail: The agent iterates against the scoring harness and reads its failure output, and the headline is the pass rate on that same harness.
'100% completion' means the visible harness passes, not that the specification is met (the authors concede this in §5).
One run; the iteration count to convergence is a single trajectory.
Repository-as-state with an evaluator gate restates the authors' SATLUTION/ABCEvo loop on RTL artifacts; the 'first to complete all suites' claim rests on the unbounded, grader-visible protocol.

coi.detail: Three of the four authors co-authored the CVDP benchmark (Pinckney et al. 2025) and report their own system topping it, with no independent replication. The backbone model is not an NVIDIA product.

verdict_reason: The headline 100% is convergence against the scoring harness itself, with no hidden tests, no baselines, one model and one run, and a ChipBench task that fails but is counted as resolved. The candid limitations section does not repair this: no claim beyond 'the loop can be driven until the visible grader passes' is supported. The domain is also hardware RTL.
applicability: Does not transfer as evidence. The design resembles what a harness stamps: a Markdown spec compiled into domain notes, an executable evaluator, an acceptance predicate and a git policy. The useful lesson is the authors' own warning. If the agent can read the acceptance tests' failure output during repair, a green gate only means it passes the visible tests. For the team's spec-driven flow, keep a held-out acceptance check (for example contract or acceptance tests the agent cannot see or edit) separate from the repair loop.
